2. De-nitrogenation–fluorination cascade
To achieve highly optimized 2e⁻ ORR catalysis suggested by the Statistical-learning-assisted
screening of active sites, nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) were
mixed in different ratios and annealed under Ar to induce a de-nitrogenation–fluorination (De-N–
F) cascade, yielding (N, F)-codoped carbon (NFC) via F-induced defect passivation (Figure 2a).
During high-temperature annealing, PVDF undergoes dehydrofluorination, releasing reactive
hydrogen fluoride (HF),25 which attacks N-sites in NC and tunes the electronic structure of the
active sites. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) confirms PVDF decomposition begins above
410 °C (Figure S17), guiding the selection of annealing temperatures. NC, synthesized following
our previous work,26 acts as both the carbon support to prevent PVDF melting and as the N-source,
while PVDF provides the F-dopant to realize the De-N–F cascade. X-ray diffraction (XRD)
patterns of the resulting materials (Figure S18) display the characteristic carbon (002) and (101)
reflections at ~25.2° and 43.7°,27 with no PVDF-related peaks, confirming complete PVDF
decomposition. Elemental analysis (Figure 2b) reveals a graduSal decrease in N content from 2.56
at.% (NC), 1.62 at.% (NFC ), 1.18 at.% (NFC) to R0 at.% (FC) as PVDF loading increases,

(FC), respectively. At a 1:1 NC/PVDF ratio (FIC sample), N is completely removed, and F content
reaches its maximum, indicating aggressive interaction of F atoms with N-sites during annealing,
leading to the elimination of N and the simultaneous incorporation of F dopant. Moreover, F
incorporation is highly temperature-sensitive: at a 1:1 NC/PVDF ratio (Figure S19g), F content
decreases from 11.1 at.% (500 °C) to 3.75 at.% (600 °C) and completely vanishes at 700 °C
(NFC600-1/1 and NFC700-1/1 samples are named as FC2 and Blank-C, respectively, Figure S20),
consistent with enhanced dehydrofluorination at elevated temperatures.28
DFT calculations of the formation energy of different N- or F-containing configurations were
performed to further understand the De-nitrogenation–fluorination process (Figure 2c). Notably,
the formation energy for F attacking graphite-N (F-A-Gra-N) is as high as 5.68 eV. While the
formation energies for F attacking two pyridinic-N sites (F-A-Pyri-N-1, or F-A-Pyri-N-2) and one
pyrrolic-N site (F-A-Pyrr-N) are 2.71 eV, 0.18 eV, and –1.45 eV, respectively, indicating that
pyrrolic-N sites are considerably more susceptible to F compared to pyridinic-N. This result
indicates that three N-species follow the stability order: graphite-N > pyridinic-N > pyrrolic-N.
The stability order can be explained as follows. Pyridinic-N is incorporated in a six-membered
ring and well matched to the graphene lattice; its lone pair occupies a sp2 orbital in the ring plane
and does not contribute to the π system, enabling a rigid sp2 framework with stronger C–N bonding.
By contrast, pyrrolic-N resides in a five-membered ring that imposes intrinsic topological strain;
its lone-pair electrons participate in the π-conjugated system, which redistributes electron density,
weakens the σ C–N bonds, and creates a chemically vulnerable, electron-rich defect motif. As a
result, pyrrolic-N is energetically more prone to being attackeSd and reconstructed, making it the
most susceptible N species during F-induced defect pasRsivation, while pyridinic-N and especially
graphitic-N embedded in a more rigid sp2 network are comparatively stable.
Further experimental characterizations, Iincluding X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS)
and X-ray Absorption Near-Edge Structure (XANES), were performed to confirm the stability

## Methods

1. Materials
Unless otherwise specified, all analytical-grade chemicals were purchased from Fisher
Scientific. Ultrapure water with a resistivity of 18.2 MΩ·cm-1 was used for preparing all solutions.
Commercial PdPt/C (75 wt% PdPt nanoparticles supported on activated carbon) obtained from
Fuel Cell Store was employed as the reference catalyst for methanol oxidation. Nafion solution
(5.0 wt%) and carbon paper (Freudenberg H23C2, Fuel Cell Store) were also supplied by Fuel Cell
Store. The PiperION anion exchange membrane (40 μm) was purchased from Versogen.

2. Synthesis of the nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) precursor
All the chemicals were used as received without any purification. The synthesis of NC was
based on our previous study.26 Typically, 3 g of XC72 was first ground for 30 min to obtain the
carbon powder; then 150 mL concentrated HNO was mixed with the carbon powder, and the
3
mixture was heated to 135℃ for 5 h. After the oxygen functionalized process, the oxygen-doped
carbon (O-XC72) is centrifuged (8000 g) and washed with plenty of water and alcohol. The
separated O-XC72 is then dried in a vacuum oven for 10 h. Then, in order to realize the nitrogen
doping, 400 mg of the intermediate O-XC72 and 2 g of melamine were mixed and ground for 30
min to obtain a uniform mixture. Then the mixture was annealed at 900 °C for 2 h under an Ar
(argon) atmosphere to get the nitrogen-doped carbon (NC).

3. Synthesis of the (N, F)-codopIed carbon (NFCs), F-doped carbons (FCs), and Blank-C
without N and F doping
All the chemicals were used as received without any purification. The synthesized NC was
mixed with varying amounts of PVDF at mass ratios of 1:1, 2:1, and 4:1 to achieve different F
contents. The resulting mixtures were then transferred to a tube furnace and annealed at 500 °C for
1 h under an Ar atmosphere to yield the materials. These products were designated as FC (NFC500-
1/1), NFC(NFC500-2/1), and NFC (NFC500-4/1), respectively. For the preparation of FCs and
control
Blank-C with different F contents, the NC and PVDF mixture at a 1:1 mass ratio was further
annealed at 600 °C (named as FC2). To completely remove the F dopant, the same NC/PVDF 1:1
mixture was annealed at 700 °C, which is named blank-C. Importantly, Blank-C does not contain
either N or F dopants.

4. Preparation and storage of electrolyte
All electrolytes were prepared using high-purity chemicals. The 0.1 M KOH solution was
prepared by dissolving 2.81 g of KOH in approximately 400 mL of ultrapure water. After complete
dissolution and cooling to room temperature, the solution was transferred to a 500 mL volumetric
flask and diluted to volume with ultrapure water. The 1.0 M KOH solution was prepared following
the same procedure using 28.06 g of anhydrous KOH and diluted to 500 mL. For the 1.0 M KOH
+ 2.0 M MeOH mixed electrolyte, 28.06 g of anhydrous KOH was first dissolved in approximately
350–400 mL of ultrapure water, followed by the addition of 40.5 mL of methanol. After thorough
mixing, the solution was transferred to a 500 mL volumetric flask and diluted to 500 mL with
ultrapure water. All solutions were thoroughly mixed and stored in sealed containers at room
temperature. The measured pH values of 0.1 M KOH, 1.0 M KOH, and 1.0 M KOH + 2.0 M
MeOH electrolytes were 13.1 ± 0.2, 13.9± 0.2, 13.8± 0.2, respectively.

The laser beam was focused onto the sample through the quartz window to collect the Raman
spectra. Chronoamperometry was used to apply a series of potentials to the working electrode, in
100 mV increments ranging from 0.1 V to 0.9 V vs. RHE.

13. Quantum Mechanical Modeling Details
To investigate the atomistic and electronic structures of N-doped, F-doped, and (N, F)-
codoped electrocatalysts for 2e- ORR toward the H O production and their complexes with the
2 2
OOH* adsorbates, periodic spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT)62 was applied using
Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) 6.3.0 with the projector augmented‐wave (PAW)
method63-66. To mimic the working environment of the electrocatalyst, the implicit solvation model
was implemented using VASPsol67. VASPKIT 1.4.068 was used to generate VASP input files and
perform post-calculation analyses. Each computational box was designed to assume a 6 × 6 × 1
hexagonal supercell with a = b = 15 Å and c = 15 Å.
Geometry optimizations of doped graphene-based models and their adsorption complexes
were performed using the Revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE)69 exchange–correlation (XC)
functional along with the D3 empirical van der Waals correction 70,71 as well as 3 × 3 × 1
Monkhorst–Pack meshes for K-point sampling of the Brillouin zone and a cut-off energy of 500
eV for the plane-wave basis set. The convergence criterion for each geometry optimization was set
to 0.01 eV/ Å for force, and the convergence criterion for each self-consistent field (SCF) cycle
was set to 1.0 × 10–6 eV for energy. The above-mentioned dimensions of a and b were obtained
from optimizations for doped graphene catalysts and fixed for adsorption complexes. All possible
adsorption sites were given in Figures S1-S3 and Table S1. To determine whether an adsorption
was successful, the distance between the OOH* adsorbate and the adsorption site was measured,
and only complexes with a distance below 2 Å were considered successful. Vibrational analyses
were performed using the finite-displacement method (IBRIOSN = 5) implemented in VASP, from
which ZPE corrections were obtained. Projected density of states (PDOS) was calculated from
site- and orbital-projected wavefunction data in VASP and analyzed using VASPKIT. To examine
the stability of the electrode material, ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were
conducted at 298.15 K using an NVT ensemble with an Andersen thermostat. Each system was
sampled for 5 ps with a 1 fs time step while keeping the simulation cell fixed. Electronic-structure
settings followed those used in the static calculations. The initial equilibration segment was
excluded from analysis; the steady segment was used to assess structural and bonding stability
over time.

13.2. Bond lengths for stability distinction between ionic and semi-ionic C–F bonds
Upon structural optimization, two distinct types of C–F bonds were identified in the
fluorinated graphene systems (Figure S4-S5). Bonds with lengths of approximately 1.50 Å
correspond to ionic C–F interactions, which are thermodynamically unstable, prone to hydrolysis,
and rarely observed in experimental characterizations due to the absence of a significant C–F ionic
peak in XPS spectra. In contrast, bonds with lengths around 1.36 Å are characteristic of semi-ionic
C–F bonds, which exhibit enhanced stability and are consistent with experimental evidence
showing that C–F bonding in such systems predominantly exists in a semi-ionic form. Therefore,
in subsequent OOH* adsorption energy calculations, only the configurations containing semi-ionic
C–F bonds are considered, while those involving ionic C–F bonds are excluded from further
analysis. This selection ensures that the computational models reflect the experimentally relevant
bonding environment, thereby improving the reliability and interpretability of the calculated
reaction energetics.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript presents a comprehensive study integrating statistical learning, theoretical calculation, materials synthesis, operando spectroscopy, and electrolyzer testing to investigate fluorine-induced defect passivation in nitrogen-doped carbons for selective 2e− ORR toward H2O2 production. The work has potential significance for both mechanistic understanding and practical electrosynthesis. However, despite the strengths, several aspects of the manuscript require substantial revision. Firstly, the central claim regarding “F-induced defect passivation as the dominant factor governing activity and stability” is not yet fully supported by the current set of evidence. The statistical-learning framework, although interesting, is complex and at times insufficiently validated experimentally, which weakens the connection between theoretical screening and real catalyst behavior. Secondly, several mechanistic interpretations, particularly those related to Raman assignment of OOH* species, surface charge reversal, and the proposed built-in electric field, need clearer justification and additional controls. Finally, the techno-economic analysis relies heavily on assumptions that should be more explicitly stated, discussed, and critically assessed.
Overall, the manuscript contains many promising elements, but the mechanistic claims, data interpretation, and contextual analysis require deeper clarification and additional experimental or analytical support. Addressing these issues will substantially enhance the scientific rigor and persuasiveness of the work. Therefore, this reviewer believes the work does not meet the high standards of Nature Communications, particularly regarding material design and catalytic mechanism. This manuscript cannot be considered for publication in Nature Communications. The detailed comments are as follows.
1. The Introduction should be more concise and logically structured. Although the current background section contains substantial information, it does not sufficiently contextualize prior knowledge or clarify the remaining gaps. Numerous sites on carbon materials, including edge carbons (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2019, 58, 1100-1105; Adv. Funct. Mater. 2023, 33, 2305795), intrinsic defects (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 21, 11589-11598; J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2022, 13, 8914-8920), and heteroatom-doped sites (Nat. Commun. 2021, 12, 4225; Adv. Energy Mater. 2024, 2304418; Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 4430), have already been identified as potential active sites for the 2e− ORR. These points should be incorporated into the discussion. In addition, the use of F-doped carbon in the 2e− ORR is not new (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202503626; Adv. Mater. 2023, 35, 2208533). Given this situation, I recommend that the authors reorganize and strengthen the introduction to better articulate the novelty of this work. The discussion should clearly progress from the challenge of poorly controlled defect states in metal-free carbon, to the rationale behind fluorine-induced defect passivation, and finally to how this study addresses unresolved mechanistic questions and fills the existing knowledge gap.
2. The statistical-learning section would benefit from clearer summarization. Figure 1 contains many descriptors and correlation analyses. A more intuitive explanatory paragraph in the main text would help readers grasp the key structure–activity insights without frequent consultation of supplementary tables.
3. The discussion of F attacking different N species could be expanded. Figure 2c suggests that pyrrolic-N is most vulnerable, yet the experimental validation is relatively brief. Additional spectral evidence (e.g., fitting residuals of N 1s or differential N K-edge spectra) would strengthen the conclusion.
4. The peak assignments in the Raman spectra require support from appropriate literature or reference databases. In addition, previous studies indicate that an adsorbed O2 species typically exhibits a characteristic band within the range of 1000 to 1200 cm-1 (Nano Lett. 2024, 24, 1650-1659; Adv. Mater. 2025, 2415712; Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 983). Therefore, it is not appropriate to attribute all features in this region solely to the OOH* intermediate.
5. The zeta-potential discussion should distinguish global surface charge from local electronic modulation. The observed shift from positive to negative charge is described qualitatively. Incorporating DOS or Bader charge comparison between NC and NFC would more rigorously support the claim of charge-state reversal and its influence on selectivity.
6. Normalizing activity using ECSA (Figure 4e) requires clarification of its validity. The double-layer capacitance of carbon materials does not necessarily correlate with the density of intrinsic active sites, particularly because fluorine doping may change the hydrophilicity or hydrophobicity of the surface and thus alter the measured ECSA. A brief explanation of the rationale for using Cdl as a proxy, along with its limitations, would improve the scientific rigor of the analysis.
7. Post-stability structural characterizations are encouraged. After long-term operation (Figure 4g), XPS, Raman, or TEM analyses of the used NFC catalyst would directly validate the retention of F-induced defect passivation.
8. Key techno-economic assumptions should be explicitly summarized in the main text. Although details are in the Supplementary Information, the economic analysis would be clearer if electricity cost, methanol price, and system-scale assumptions were briefly stated.
9. Based on the RRDE-derived LSV curves (Figure 4a) and the corresponding H2O2 selectivity (Figure 4c), the improvement gained from fluorine doping (NFC) appears minimal, and the enhancement over the NC sample is not clearly demonstrated. This weak correlation with the authors' theoretical predictions reduces the overall persuasiveness of the work.
Some minor comments:
1. Consistency of notation and symbols across figures should be improved. Some abbreviations (e.g., ORR//MOR vs ORR//OER) differ slightly in formatting across figures, and ΔGOOH* appears with inconsistent styling. Unifying these will improve clarity and professionalism.
2. The conclusion could more clearly highlight the methodological contribution. Beyond material development, the combined use of statistical learning, DFT calculations, operando spectroscopy, and flow-cell validation forms an integrated framework that can be applied to other catalytic systems. Explicitly emphasizing this transferable aspect would strengthen the overall impact of the work.

DFT calculations of the formation energy of different N- or F-containing configurations were
performed to further understand the De-nitrogenation–fluorination process (Figure 2c). Notably,
the formation energy for F attacking graphite-N (F-A-Gra-N) is as high as 5.68 eV. While the
formation energies for F attacking two pyridinic-N sites (F-A-Pyri-N-1, or F-A-Pyri-N-2) and one
pyrrolic-N site (F-A-Pyrr-N) are 2.71 eV, 0.18 eV, and –1.45 eV, respectively, indicating that
pyrrolic-N sites are considerably more susceptible to F compared to pyridinic-N. This result
indicates that three N-species follow the stability order: graphite-N > pyridinic-N > pyrrolic-N.
The stability order can be explained as follows. Pyridinic-N is incorporated in a six-membered
ring and well matched to the graphene lattice; its lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane
and does not contribute to the π system, enabling a rigid sp2 framework with stronger C–N bonding.
By contrast, pyrrolic-N resides in a five-membered ring that imposes intrinsic topological strain;
its lone-pair electrons participate in the π-conjugated system, which redistributes electron density,
weakens the σ C–N bonds, and creates a chemically vulnerable, electron-rich defect motif. As a
result, pyrrolic-N is energetically more prone to being attacked and reconstruction, making it the
most susceptible N species during F-induced defect passivation, while pyridinic-N and especially
graphitic-N embedded in a more rigid sp² network are comparatively stable.

## Introduction

Hydrogen peroxide (H O ) is widely employed in many crucial industries, such as
2 2
semiconductor manufacturing, wastewater treatment, and chemical synthesis.1,2 Electrosynthesis
of H O using two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e⁻ ORR) offers a sustainable and
2 2
decentralized alternative to the traditional anthraquinone oxidation (AO) process.2,3 The key to
efficient 2e⁻ ORR lies in precisely regulating the adsorption of the OOH* intermediate on
catalytically active sites (ASs).4 Strong OOH* binding favors the competing four-electron (4e-
ORR) pathway to H O,5 whereas weak binding limits OOH* formation and stability.6 Therefore,
2
Precise prediction and regulation of OOH* adsorption energy is essential for efficient catalyst
screening and the commercialization of H O electrosynthesis. Both metal-based and metal-free
2 2
carbon catalysts have been explored for selective 2e⁻ ORR.2,3,7,8 Metal-based catalysts, particularly
transition-metal single-atom or dual-atom sites, benefit Sfrom well-defined coordination
environments that enable relatively straightforward perfRormance prediction.9,10 On the other hand,
metal-free catalysts offer intrinsic advantages over metal catalysts, including lower cost, higher
abundance, corrosion resistance, and eliminatIion of metal leaching, making them highly attractive
for large-scale, sustainable H O production. Over the past decade, extensive efforts have
2 2
identified a variety of active motifs in carbon-based materials capable of promoting the 2e⁻ ORR.
These include edge carbon atoms with unsaturated coordination,11,12 intrinsic defect sites such as
vacancies and topological distortions,13,14 and heteroatom-doped configurations15-17 that modulate
local electronic structures. Such sites can generate localized charge or spin densities favorable for
OOH* adsorption, enabling selective H O formation. Despite these advances, a fundamental
2 2
challenge persists in metal-free carbon catalysts: the poor controllability of defect states. Especially,
the heteroatom-doped carbon catalysts exhibit significant atomic heterogeneity due to diverse
dopant motifs and random defects, making it challenging to correlate structure with catalytic
performance. Although heteroatom-induced defects (e.g., pyrrolic N, pyridinic N, and dangling
bonds) are widely recognized as active sites, the catalytic role of these defects under the influences
of secondary heteroatom doping and partial defect passivation remained poorly understood.3,17
Achieving defect passivation typically requires restoring sp2 conjugation or incorporating
heteroatoms that terminate defect states; however, perfect carbons often display poor 2e⁻ ORR
activity, and excessive heteroatom doping may introduce new defects rather than passivate existing
ones.18 Elements with multiple bonding configurations could enable defect passivation,19,20 while
likely preserving catalytic activity towards 2e⁻ ORR. Beyond activity, stability is equally critical
for practical H O production, as edge defects with high local electron density are prone to
2 2
hydroxyl radical (•OH) attack, leading to performance decay.21 Transferring the local high electron
density to more stable sites and terminating the dangling bondsS can enhance the chemical stability
and reduce the tendency to be attacked, and finally Rincrease the stability. From this defect-
engineering perspective, fluorine (F) emerges as a r ational yet underexplored choice.
As the most electronegative element, F fIorms multi-bonding states and exhibits pronounced
electron-withdrawing capability, suggesting its potential to terminate unstable dangling bonds and
redistribute local charge density. Although F doping shows some potential as a conventional
electronic dopant in 2e⁻ ORR catalysts,22,23 its interaction with pre-existing defect motifs,
particularly N-related defects, has not been thoroughly studied, leading to a significant knowledge
gap in the design of metal-free catalysts. Particularly, several unresolved mechanistic questions
remain: How does F interact with different nitrogen configurations and defect states? Can F-
induced defect passivation be translated into predictable regulation of OOH* adsorption? And how
does such passivation simultaneously impact selectivity and long-term durability? Addressing
these questions is essential for establishing a unified structure–activity relationship for F-modified
carbon catalysts.
In this work, to elucidate the unclear role of defect passivation in governing catalytic activity

passivation. We constructed 15 graphene configurations with and without defect passivation by
systematically varying N and F dopants, and performed DFT calculations on 66 potential active

indicate that F passivation significantly reduces the free energy of OOH* (∆G ), thereby

2. De-nitrogenation–fluorination cascade
To achieve highly optimized 2e⁻ ORR catalysis suggested by the Statistical-learning-assisted
screening of active sites, nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) were
mixed in different ratios and annealed under Ar to induce a de-nitrogenation–fluorination (De-N–
F) cascade, yielding (N, F)-codoped carbon (NFC) via F-induced defect passivation (Figure 2a).
During high-temperature annealing, PVDF undergoes dehydrofluorination, releasing reactive
hydrogen fluoride (HF),25 which attacks N-sites in NC and tunes the electronic structure of the
active sites. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) confirms PVDF decomposition begins above
410 °C (Figure S17), guiding the selection of annealing temperatures. NC, synthesized following
our previous work,26 acts as both the carbon support to prevent PVDF melting and as the N-source,
while PVDF provides the F-dopant to realize the De-N–F cascade. X-ray diffraction (XRD)
patterns of the resulting materials (Figure S18) display the characteristic carbon (002) and (101)
reflections at ~25.2° and 43.7°,27 with no PVDF-related peaks, confirming complete PVDF
decomposition. Elemental analysis (Figure 2b) reveals a graduSal decrease in N content from 2.56
at.% (NC), 1.62 at.% (NFC ), 1.18 at.% (NFC) to R0 at.% (FC) as PVDF loading increases,

reaches its maximum, indicating aggressive interaction of F atoms with N-sites during annealing,
leading to the elimination of N and the simultaneous incorporation of F dopant. Moreover, F
incorporation is highly temperature-sensitive: at a 1:1 NC/PVDF ratio (Figure S19g), F content
decreases from 11.1 at.% (500 °C) to 3.75 at.% (600 °C) and completely vanishes at 700 °C
(NFC600-1/1 and NFC700-1/1 samples are named as FC2 and Blank-C, respectively, Figure S20),
consistent with enhanced dehydrofluorination at elevated temperatures.28
DFT calculations of the formation energy of different N- or F-containing configurations were
performed to further understand the De-nitrogenation–fluorination process (Figure 2c). Notably,
the formation energy for F attacking graphite-N (F-A-Gra-N) is as high as 5.68 eV. While the
formation energies for F attacking two pyridinic-N sites (F-A-Pyri-N-1, or F-A-Pyri-N-2) and one
pyrrolic-N site (F-A-Pyrr-N) are 2.71 eV, 0.18 eV, and –1.45 eV, respectively, indicating that
pyrrolic-N sites are considerably more susceptible to F compared to pyridinic-N. This result
indicates that three N-species follow the stability order: graphite-N > pyridinic-N > pyrrolic-N.
The stability order can be explained as follows. Pyridinic-N is incorporated in a six-membered
ring and well matched to the graphene lattice; its lone pair occupies a sp2 orbital in the ring plane
and does not contribute to the π system, enabling a rigid sp2 framework with stronger C–N bonding.
By contrast, pyrrolic-N resides in a five-membered ring that imposes intrinsic topological strain;
its lone-pair electrons participate in the π-conjugated system, which redistributes electron density,
weakens the σ C–N bonds, and creates a chemically vulnerable, electron-rich defect motif. As a
result, pyrrolic-N is energetically more prone to being attackeSd and reconstructed, making it the
most susceptible N species during F-induced defect pasRsivation, while pyridinic-N and especially
graphitic-N embedded in a more rigid sp2 network are comparatively stable.

7. 2e− ORR paired with methanol oxidation for high economic benefits

## Methods

1. Materials
Unless otherwise specified, all analytical-grade chemicals were purchased from Fisher
Scientific. Ultrapure water with a resistivity of 18.2 MΩ·cm-1 was used for preparing all solutions.
Commercial PdPt/C (75 wt% PdPt nanoparticles supported on activated carbon) obtained from
Fuel Cell Store was employed as the reference catalyst for methanol oxidation. Nafion solution
(5.0 wt%) and carbon paper (Freudenberg H23C2, Fuel Cell Store) were also supplied by Fuel Cell
Store. The PiperION anion exchange membrane (40 μm) was purchased from Versogen.

2. Synthesis of the nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) precursor
All the chemicals were used as received without any purification. The synthesis of NC was
based on our previous study.26 Typically, 3 g of XC72 was first ground for 30 min to obtain the
carbon powder; then 150 mL concentrated HNO was mixed with the carbon powder, and the
3
mixture was heated to 135℃ for 5 h. After the oxygen functionalized process, the oxygen-doped
carbon (O-XC72) is centrifuged (8000 g) and washed with plenty of water and alcohol. The
separated O-XC72 is then dried in a vacuum oven for 10 h. Then, in order to realize the nitrogen
doping, 400 mg of the intermediate O-XC72 and 2 g of melamine were mixed and ground for 30
min to obtain a uniform mixture. Then the mixture was annealed at 900 °C for 2 h under an Ar
(argon) atmosphere to get the nitrogen-doped carbon (NC).

3. Synthesis of the (N, F)-codopIed carbon (NFCs), F-doped carbons (FCs), and Blank-C
without N and F doping
All the chemicals were used as received without any purification. The synthesized NC was
mixed with varying amounts of PVDF at mass ratios of 1:1, 2:1, and 4:1 to achieve different F
contents. The resulting mixtures were then transferred to a tube furnace and annealed at 500 °C for
1 h under an Ar atmosphere to yield the materials. These products were designated as FC (NFC500-
1/1), NFC(NFC500-2/1), and NFC (NFC500-4/1), respectively. For the preparation of FCs and
control
Blank-C with different F contents, the NC and PVDF mixture at a 1:1 mass ratio was further
annealed at 600 °C (named as FC2). To completely remove the F dopant, the same NC/PVDF 1:1
mixture was annealed at 700 °C, which is named blank-C. Importantly, Blank-C does not contain
either N or F dopants.

4. Preparation and storage of electrolyte
All electrolytes were prepared using high-purity chemicals. The 0.1 M KOH solution was
prepared by dissolving 2.81 g of KOH in approximately 400 mL of ultrapure water. After complete
dissolution and cooling to room temperature, the solution was transferred to a 500 mL volumetric
flask and diluted to volume with ultrapure water. The 1.0 M KOH solution was prepared following
the same procedure using 28.06 g of anhydrous KOH and diluted to 500 mL. For the 1.0 M KOH
+ 2.0 M MeOH mixed electrolyte, 28.06 g of anhydrous KOH was first dissolved in approximately
350–400 mL of ultrapure water, followed by the addition of 40.5 mL of methanol. After thorough
mixing, the solution was transferred to a 500 mL volumetric flask and diluted to 500 mL with
ultrapure water. All solutions were thoroughly mixed and stored in sealed containers at room
temperature. The measured pH values of 0.1 M KOH, 1.0 M KOH, and 1.0 M KOH + 2.0 M
MeOH electrolytes were 13.1 ± 0.2, 13.9± 0.2, 13.8± 0.2, respectively.

Nano equipped with a 532 nm streamline laser excitation source. The electrochemical cell,
featuring a quartz window, accommodated the working electrode (the obtained catalyst), a

The laser beam was focused onto the sample through the quartz window to collect the Raman
spectra. Chronoamperometry was used to apply a series of potentials to the working electrode, in
100 mV increments ranging from 0.1 V to 0.9 V vs. RHE.

13. Quantum Mechanical Modeling Details
To investigate the atomistic and electronic structures of N-doped, F-doped, and (N, F)-
codoped electrocatalysts for 2e- ORR toward the H O production and their complexes with the
2 2
OOH* adsorbates, periodic spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT)62 was applied using
Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) 6.3.0 with the projector augmented‐wave (PAW)
method63-66. To mimic the working environment of the electrocatalyst, the implicit solvation model
was implemented using VASPsol67. VASPKIT 1.4.068 was used to generate VASP input files and
perform post-calculation analyses. Each computational box was designed to assume a 6 × 6 × 1
hexagonal supercell with a = b = 15 Å and c = 15 Å.
Geometry optimizations of doped graphene-based models and their adsorption complexes
were performed using the Revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE)69 exchange–correlation (XC)
functional along with the D3 empirical van der Waals correction 70,71 as well as 3 × 3 × 1
Monkhorst–Pack meshes for K-point sampling of the Brillouin zone and a cut-off energy of 500
eV for the plane-wave basis set. The convergence criterion for each geometry optimization was set
to 0.01 eV/ Å for force, and the convergence criterion for each self-consistent field (SCF) cycle
was set to 1.0 × 10–6 eV for energy. The above-mentioned dimensions of a and b were obtained
from optimizations for doped graphene catalysts and fixed for adsorption complexes. All possible
adsorption sites were given in Figures S1-S3 and Table S1. To determine whether an adsorption
was successful, the distance between the OOH* adsorbate and the adsorption site was measured,
and only complexes with a distance below 2 Å were considered successful. Vibrational analyses
were performed using the finite-displacement method (IBRIOSN = 5) implemented in VASP, from
which ZPE corrections were obtained. Projected density of states (PDOS) was calculated from
site- and orbital-projected wavefunction data in VASP and analyzed using VASPKIT. To examine
the stability of the electrode material, ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were
conducted at 298.15 K using an NVT ensemble with an Andersen thermostat. Each system was
sampled for 5 ps with a 1 fs time step while keeping the simulation cell fixed. Electronic-structure
settings followed those used in the static calculations. The initial equilibration segment was
excluded from analysis; the steady segment was used to assess structural and bonding stability
over time.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript presents a comprehensive study integrating statistical learning, theoretical calculation, materials synthesis, operando spectroscopy, and electrolyzer testing to investigate fluorine-induced defect passivation in nitrogen-doped carbons for selective 2e− ORR toward H2O2 production. The work has potential significance for both mechanistic understanding and practical electrosynthesis. However, despite the strengths, several aspects of the manuscript require substantial revision. Firstly, the central claim regarding “F-induced defect passivation as the dominant factor governing activity and stability” is not yet fully supported by the current set of evidence. The statistical-learning framework, although interesting, is complex and at times insufficiently validated experimentally, which weakens the connection between theoretical screening and real catalyst behavior. Secondly, several mechanistic interpretations, particularly those related to Raman assignment of OOH* species, surface charge reversal, and the proposed built-in electric field, need clearer justification and additional controls. Finally, the techno-economic analysis relies heavily on assumptions that should be more explicitly stated, discussed, and critically assessed.
Overall, the manuscript contains many promising elements, but the mechanistic claims, data interpretation, and contextual analysis require deeper clarification and additional experimental or analytical support. Addressing these issues will substantially enhance the scientific rigor and persuasiveness of the work. Therefore, this reviewer believes the work does not meet the high standards of Nature Communications, particularly regarding material design and catalytic mechanism. This manuscript cannot be considered for publication in Nature Communications. The detailed comments are as follows.
1. The Introduction should be more concise and logically structured. Although the current background section contains substantial information, it does not sufficiently contextualize prior knowledge or clarify the remaining gaps. Numerous sites on carbon materials, including edge carbons (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2019, 58, 1100-1105; Adv. Funct. Mater. 2023, 33, 2305795), intrinsic defects (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 21, 11589-11598; J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2022, 13, 8914-8920), and heteroatom-doped sites (Nat. Commun. 2021, 12, 4225; Adv. Energy Mater. 2024, 2304418; Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 4430), have already been identified as potential active sites for the 2e− ORR. These points should be incorporated into the discussion. In addition, the use of F-doped carbon in the 2e− ORR is not new (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202503626; Adv. Mater. 2023, 35, 2208533). Given this situation, I recommend that the authors reorganize and strengthen the introduction to better articulate the novelty of this work. The discussion should clearly progress from the challenge of poorly controlled defect states in metal-free carbon, to the rationale behind fluorine-induced defect passivation, and finally to how this study addresses unresolved mechanistic questions and fills the existing knowledge gap.
2. The statistical-learning section would benefit from clearer summarization. Figure 1 contains many descriptors and correlation analyses. A more intuitive explanatory paragraph in the main text would help readers grasp the key structure–activity insights without frequent consultation of supplementary tables.
3. The discussion of F attacking different N species could be expanded. Figure 2c suggests that pyrrolic-N is most vulnerable, yet the experimental validation is relatively brief. Additional spectral evidence (e.g., fitting residuals of N 1s or differential N K-edge spectra) would strengthen the conclusion.
4. The peak assignments in the Raman spectra require support from appropriate literature or reference databases. In addition, previous studies indicate that an adsorbed O2 species typically exhibits a characteristic band within the range of 1000 to 1200 cm-1 (Nano Lett. 2024, 24, 1650-1659; Adv. Mater. 2025, 2415712; Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 983). Therefore, it is not appropriate to attribute all features in this region solely to the OOH* intermediate.
5. The zeta-potential discussion should distinguish global surface charge from local electronic modulation. The observed shift from positive to negative charge is described qualitatively. Incorporating DOS or Bader charge comparison between NC and NFC would more rigorously support the claim of charge-state reversal and its influence on selectivity.
6. Normalizing activity using ECSA (Figure 4e) requires clarification of its validity. The double-layer capacitance of carbon materials does not necessarily correlate with the density of intrinsic active sites, particularly because fluorine doping may change the hydrophilicity or hydrophobicity of the surface and thus alter the measured ECSA. A brief explanation of the rationale for using Cdl as a proxy, along with its limitations, would improve the scientific rigor of the analysis.
7. Post-stability structural characterizations are encouraged. After long-term operation (Figure 4g), XPS, Raman, or TEM analyses of the used NFC catalyst would directly validate the retention of F-induced defect passivation.
8. Key techno-economic assumptions should be explicitly summarized in the main text. Although details are in the Supplementary Information, the economic analysis would be clearer if electricity cost, methanol price, and system-scale assumptions were briefly stated.
9. Based on the RRDE-derived LSV curves (Figure 4a) and the corresponding H2O2 selectivity (Figure 4c), the improvement gained from fluorine doping (NFC) appears minimal, and the enhancement over the NC sample is not clearly demonstrated. This weak correlation with the authors' theoretical predictions reduces the overall persuasiveness of the work.
Some minor comments:
1. Consistency of notation and symbols across figures should be improved. Some abbreviations (e.g., ORR//MOR vs ORR//OER) differ slightly in formatting across figures, and ΔGOOH* appears with inconsistent styling. Unifying these will improve clarity and professionalism.
2. The conclusion could more clearly highlight the methodological contribution. Beyond material development, the combined use of statistical learning, DFT calculations, operando spectroscopy, and flow-cell validation forms an integrated framework that can be applied to other catalytic systems. Explicitly emphasizing this transferable aspect would strengthen the overall impact of the work.

DFT calculations of the formation energy of different N- or F-containing configurations were
performed to further understand the De-nitrogenation–fluorination process (Figure 2c). Notably,
the formation energy for F attacking graphite-N (F-A-Gra-N) is as high as 5.68 eV. While the
formation energies for F attacking two pyridinic-N sites (F-A-Pyri-N-1, or F-A-Pyri-N-2) and one
pyrrolic-N site (F-A-Pyrr-N) are 2.71 eV, 0.18 eV, and –1.45 eV, respectively, indicating that
pyrrolic-N sites are considerably more susceptible to F compared to pyridinic-N. This result
indicates that three N-species follow the stability order: graphite-N > pyridinic-N > pyrrolic-N.
The stability order can be explained as follows. Pyridinic-N is incorporated in a six-membered
ring and well matched to the graphene lattice; its lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane
and does not contribute to the π system, enabling a rigid sp2 framework with stronger C–N bonding.
By contrast, pyrrolic-N resides in a five-membered ring that imposes intrinsic topological strain;
its lone-pair electrons participate in the π-conjugated system, which redistributes electron density,
weakens the σ C–N bonds, and creates a chemically vulnerable, electron-rich defect motif. As a
result, pyrrolic-N is energetically more prone to being attacked and reconstruction, making it the
most susceptible N species during F-induced defect passivation, while pyridinic-N and especially
graphitic-N embedded in a more rigid sp² network are comparatively stable.
